blocks.text: 1. Persistence

blocks.alt: In-memory data is written to disk to become durable data

blocks.text: Persistence shifts focus from storage efficiency to storage durability: it covers how vector databases keep data intact across restarts.
It writes vectors to durable storage so a restart never loses them, a foundational reliability guarantee for any production system.
2. Memory Versus Disk

blocks.alt: Memory is fast and volatile while disk is slower and durable

blocks.text: Keeping vectors only in memory makes search extremely fast, but that data disappears the moment the process stops.
Persistence writes that same data somewhere durable, like disk, so it survives a restart.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Storage location","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Memory only","Extremely fast, but lost on restart"],["Persisted to disk","Durable across restarts, with some added latency"]]}

blocks.text: 3. What Gets Persisted
Both the raw vectors and their metadata, stored together as covered in What is a Vector Database, need to survive a restart.
The index structure itself often gets persisted too, which avoids a full rebuild after every restart.
4. Write Ahead Logs

blocks.alt: A write goes to the write-ahead log, then gets applied to data

blocks.text: A write ahead log records every change durably before applying it to the main data structure.
If a crash happens mid write, the log lets the system recover exactly where it left off.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A write ahead log acts like a durable receipt for every change. Even if the system crashes right after a write starts, the log provides enough information to finish or safely undo that write on restart.

blocks.text: 5. Snapshots Versus Continuous Persistence

blocks.alt: Periodic snapshots are compared against continuous persistence

blocks.text: A snapshot captures the entire dataset's state at one moment; continuous persistence writes every change as it happens.
Combining both approaches balances recovery speed against ongoing write overhead.
6. Recovery After A Failure

blocks.alt: A crash triggers replaying the write-ahead log to recover state

blocks.text: A restarted system reloads its persisted state before serving queries again.
How quickly that reload happens directly affects how long the system stays unavailable.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A system relying only on infrequent snapshots without a write ahead log risks losing every change made since the last snapshot if it crashes unexpectedly, a real gap in durability.

blocks.text: 7. Persistence Performance Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Frequent persistence is compared against fast writes

blocks.text: Writing every change durably to disk adds latency compared to keeping data purely in memory.
A pipeline needs to balance durability against raw write speed.
8. Persistence Across Replicas
Each replica, kept in sync as covered in Replication, typically maintains its own independent persisted copy.
Losing one replica's disk does not threaten the durability of the others.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Failure scenario","Outcome with persisted replicas"],"rows":[["One replica's disk fails","Other replicas' persisted copies remain intact"],["Entire system restarts","Each replica reloads its own independently persisted data"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Persistence Configuration Deserves Careful Attention

blocks.alt: Data loss being unacceptable points toward tuning persistence carefully

blocks.text: Production systems that cannot tolerate data loss need careful persistence configuration.
Disposable, easily rebuilt test data can tolerate lighter, less durable persistence instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below shows a simple write ahead log recovering an in progress write after a simulated crash.

code.content:
write_ahead_log = []
main_store = {}

def write_with_log(key, value):
    # record the write in the log before applying it
    write_ahead_log.append({"key": key, "value": value, "applied": False})
    # simulate applying the write to the main store
    main_store[key] = value
    write_ahead_log[-1]["applied"] = True

def recover_from_log(write_ahead_log, main_store):
    # replay any entries that never finished applying
    for entry in write_ahead_log:
        if not entry["applied"]:
            print(f"  Recovering unfinished write: {entry['key']} -> {entry['value']}")
            main_store[entry["key"]] = entry["value"]
            entry["applied"] = True

write_with_log("chunk_1", "original text")
write_with_log("chunk_2", "second entry")

# simulate a crash mid write, leaving the last entry unapplied
write_ahead_log.append({"key": "chunk_3", "value": "interrupted write", "applied": False})

print("Main store before recovery:", main_store)
recover_from_log(write_ahead_log, main_store)
print("Main store after recovery:", main_store)

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the interrupted write recovered and applied during the recovery step, ensuring no change is silently lost.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Keeping vectors only in memory for a production system that cannot tolerate data loss.
Relying only on infrequent snapshots without a write ahead log to cover the gap between them.
Ignoring the latency cost persistence adds compared to purely in memory operation.
Assuming replication alone guarantees durability without each replica also persisting its own data.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Persistence writes vectors to durable storage so a restart never loses them.
Memory only storage is extremely fast but disappears the moment the process stops.
Vectors, metadata, and often the index structure itself all need to be persisted.
A write ahead log records changes durably before applying them, enabling crash recovery.
Snapshots capture full state periodically; continuous persistence writes every change as it happens.
A restarted system reloads its persisted state before serving queries, affecting downtime length.
Persisting to disk adds latency compared to purely in memory operation, a real tradeoff.
Each replica typically maintains its own independent persisted copy for combined resilience.
